title: Sloth and diligence
hookLine: the monks' noonday demon: listless boredom with good things

cards: Midday in the Egyptian desert. A monk sits in his small cell. He came out here on purpose, to pray, to work, to be with God, and right now he can't stand it.
He looks out the door at the sun. It hasn't moved. He looks again.
Still hasn't moved. The day feels endless. He starts thinking another monastery would suit him better, or a visit to a brother would do him good, or maybe this whole life was a mistake.
Nothing is wrong. That's the trouble. The old monks had a name for this hour, and this feeling: acedia.

teach.b: Tradition says acedia is the old name behind the sin later called sloth, and it's a different animal from laziness. A lazy person might be happily asleep on the couch. Acedia is not happy.
It's a heavy, restless boredom with the very things that matter: prayer, work, the people in front of you.
Evagrius, a monk who lived in that desert and wrote about the thoughts that trouble monks, called it the noonday demon, and described that same monk staring at the sun, itching to be anywhere else.
Some of the monks connected it with a line in the Psalms about a destruction that wastes at noonday. Noon fits. The morning's fresh start is gone; the evening's rest is far off.
It's the long middle, where a lot of life is actually lived. The monks' cure was not a burst of effort. It was staying put.
Stay in your cell, they said. Don't run.

teach.h: STAY, AND DO THE NEXT THING.
teach.b: Do the next small thing with your hands: weave a basket, say a psalm, sweep. Scripture's blunt version: "Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise." The ant doesn't wait to feel inspired.
And Ecclesiastes: "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might." Not the great task; the one in front of you. That's diligence: not hustle, but care that keeps showing up.
Look back over this week and the same shape appears. Justice, courage, temperance, humility, kindness, patience, and now diligence: each a small, steady habit, practiced one ordinary day at a time.

how: In Christian monastic tradition, acedia is met with stability and steady work: staying in one's place, keeping the hours of prayer, and doing ordinary tasks with care; the deadly sin of sloth in later lists grew from it.

o: a deep sadness after losing someone you love
a heavy, restless boredom with good things
plain laziness, like sleeping in on a day off

games.q: the long middle of the day — tap the pairs.
p: stay put, do the next small thing
go to the ant, thou sluggard

s: acedia is just another word for laziness
it's restless, heavy boredom with the things that matter, not a happy nap.
the monks' cure for acedia was a big burst of effort
it was staying put and doing the next small thing: a basket, a psalm, a sweep.
the monks called it the noonday demon
the middle of the day, when the morning is gone and the evening is far off.

games.q: you're a desert monk at noon. the day won't move, and you're sure another monastery would be better for your soul. what do the old monks advise?
o: leave and find a better place.
stay in your cell and do the next small task.
games.why: stay. the advice was not to run, and to keep your hands busy with ordinary work and prayer until the noonday demon gives up.

practice: Notice if there's a flat, heavy feeling anywhere in your day, a thing you keep circling and not starting, and don't fight it or plan to fix your whole life. Just name the next small task: one email, one dish, one page.
If you pray, you can offer it, as the monks offered their baskets.

wordCard.voice: Acedia. The desert monks' word for listless boredom with good things, the noonday demon; the old root of sloth.

orig.note: Greek: listlessness, weariness of spirit. The desert monks' word, which tradition places behind the deadly sin of sloth.

carryVoice: Your line: the noonday demon. The monks' cure was staying put. Same time tomorrow.
